It is also (UNFORTUNATELY) not true. The Fed still answers to no-one, except very loosely to congress, who can amend the Federal Reserve Act.

The act establishing the Federal Reserve is "The Federal Reserve Act" from 1913, which has been amended dozens of times in the past century, and as recently as the 2015 FAST act (a transportation act which, among other things, means that the individual federal reserve banks (NY Fed, STL Fed, MIN Fed, SF Fed, BOS Fed, etc) must transfer deposits >10B over to the FR general fund):

https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/22?q=%7B%22search%22%3A%5B%22%5C%22FAST+act%5C%22%22%5D%7D&s=7&r=11

In 1934, the "Gold Reserve Act" transferred all the gold from the Federal Reserve to the US Treasury; and gave the Treasury and President the power to set gold prices (i.e., taking us off of the gold standard)

https://www.loc.gov/law/help/statutes-at-large/73rd-congress/session-2/c73s2ch6.pdf

It is this act that is amended by the CARES act:

https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/senate-bill/3548/text?format=txt&q=product+actualizaci%C3%B3n

(g) Conforming Amendment.--Section 10(a) of the Gold Reserve Act of 
1934 (31 U.S.C. 5302(a)) is amended--
 (1) by striking ``and'' before ``section 3''; and
 (2) by inserting ``and the Coronavirus Economic 
 Stabilization Act of 2020,'' before ``and for investing''.

Part of allowing the president to set gold prices by fiat, the Gold Act creates an arm of the Treasury empowered to buy and sell gold in order to maintain the gold value of the dollar. If the president says "an ounce of gold is now worth $2", then that arm of the treasury would engage in selling gold and gold contracts to try to maintain that parity; if the president says "an ounce of gold is now worth $5000" that arm of the treasury would be a bulk purchaser of gold at that price -- at least under the original act.

The CARES amendment appears to place a secondary structure within the treasury, and alter the Gold Reserve Act to establish that the Treasury can move funds to and from the Federal Reserve not only for maintaining gold parity, but also for activities related to the Coronavirus act of 2020.

That's all. No changes to the Fed or amendments to the Federal Reserve Act.

However, the reverse repo (e.g. buying a security from a hedgie, on the promise that they'll buy it back with some interest) side of the books increased from ~1T in Q42017 to ~1.25T in Q32019; suggesting that the draw-down of deposits was largely due to increased lending to the funding markets.

between October 2017 and August 2019, the Federal Reserve reduced its Treasury holdings at the rate of $35 to $50 billion a month, a process known as the balance sheet normalization or taper

3) JPM says to Morgan Stanley "Buy this treasury (A) from me now, I'll buy it back in 3W for 1.02x the value"
4) Morgan Stanley reduces its account balance at the FRB, transferring it to JPM in exchange for Treasury (A)
5) JPM passes the cash from Morgan Stanley over to Hedgie, transfers treasury (A) to MS, keeps treasury (B)

At this junction, both JPM and Morgan Stanley have entered into reverse-repos; so the end result looks just like figure 3. The deposits are drawn down by virtue of buying Treasury (A); and the amount of reverse-repos increases as a result of banks increasingly turning to other repo market actors to finance their own repo operations.
